claims.text: The construction industry remains one of the least automated sectors.
claims.poster_quote: The construction industry remains one of the least automated sectors, despite its economic scale and high-risk tasks—especially on roofs.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The construction industry is among the least automated sectors with respect to robotics, despite its substantial economic relevance [6].
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that the construction industry is among the least automated sectors.

claims.text: Roof work involves hazardous conditions like falls and repetitive physical labor.
claims.poster_quote: Roof work involves hazardous conditions like falls and repetitive physical labor, making it ideal for robotic automation.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Tasks such as construction, maintenance, installation, and inspection expose workers to significant risks, with slipping and falling accidents constituting a major cause of fatalities [7]. At the same time, many tasks on roofs are physically demanding and repetitive, providing a strong motivation to explore robotic assistance.
claims.reason: The paper mentions hazardous conditions like falls and repetitive physical labor in roof work.

claims.text: Quadruped robots remain underutilized in real-world applications.
claims.poster_quote: Quadruped robots, while increasingly capable, remain underutilized in real-world applications.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Although these tasks have been proposed for a long time and quadruped capabilities have rapidly advanced, commercialization and deployment in these applications remain limited.
claims.reason: The paper states that quadruped robots remain underutilized in real-world applications.

claims.text: This work investigates whether commercial quadrupeds like the Unitree Go2 can operate effectively on tiled roofs.
claims.poster_quote: This work investigates whether commercial quadrupeds like the Unitree Go2 can operate effectively on tiled roofs—a novel, unexplored environment combining steep inclines, smooth surfaces, and discrete structural features.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: This paper investigates the feasibility of deploying quadruped walking robots for the automation of work in roof environments. [...] A dedicated test rig of a roof’s surface was designed to evaluate the baseline performance of a commercial quadruped, the Unitree Go2, in this new environment.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly investigates the Unitree Go2's performance on tiled roofs.

claims.text: The goal is to establish a baseline for future development by evaluating locomotion performance, failure modes, and friction limitations.
claims.poster_quote: The goal is to establish a baseline for future development by evaluating locomotion performance, failure modes, and friction limitations.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: This work provides: [...] Quantitative failure thresholds for balanced standing, get-up/lie-down motions, and incline walking establishing a baseline for future research.
claims.reason: The paper aims to establish a baseline for future development by evaluating locomotion performance, failure modes, and friction limitations.

claims.text: A custom test rig simulating a German-style tiled roof (Frankfurther Pfanne) was built to evaluate the Unitree Go2’s performance.
claims.poster_quote: A custom test rig simulating a German-style tiled roof (Frankfurther Pfanne) was built to evaluate the Unitree Go2’s performance.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: To objectively assess the performance of the Go2 (software version 1.4.4) and create a baseline for future comparison with custom feet, an adjustable test rig of a roof environment was developed (see Fig. 1). As surface material the Frankfurther Pfanne was chosen, which is the most common type of roof tile in Germany [2].
claims.reason: The paper describes the creation of a test rig simulating a German-style tiled roof (Frankfurther Pfanne).

claims.text: Three core locomotion tasks were tested: balancing on increasing inclines, get-up/lie-down sequences in multiple orientations, and incline walking.
claims.poster_quote: Three core locomotion tasks were tested: balancing on increasing inclines, get-up/lie-down sequences in multiple orientations, and incline walking.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: With the Go2, three core skills were examined: balancing on continuously increasing inclines, get-up/lie-down sequences, and incline walking.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly lists these three locomotion tasks as being tested.

claims.text: Motion capture (OptiTrack) tracked foot slippage via reflective markers.
claims.poster_quote: Motion capture (OptiTrack) tracked foot slippage via reflective markers.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: For this purpose, the OptiTrack system – a motion capture system based on infrared light and reflective markers – is employed.
claims.reason: The paper confirms the use of OptiTrack to track foot slippage via reflective markers.

claims.text: Friction coefficients were measured using a UR10e force-torque sensor.
claims.poster_quote: Friction coefficients were measured using a UR10e force-torque sensor.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: As a preliminary experiment the dynamic coefficient of friction f of the ball feet was measured by using the internal force-torque sensor of a UR10e.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that friction coefficients were measured using a UR10e force-torque sensor.

claims.text: All trials were automated via Python using WebRTC, with the robot set to standard walking mode at 1.0 m/s.
claims.poster_quote: All trials were automated via Python using WebRTC, with the robot set to standard walking mode at 1.0 m/s.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: For high repeatability reasons, all trials were controlled via Python using the WebRTC implementation provided by Severov [16]. The robot was set to standard walking mode and a target speed of 1.0 m s−1.
claims.reason: The paper confirms that trials were automated via Python using WebRTC, with the robot set to standard walking mode at 1.0 m/s.

claims.text: Experiments were repeated 10 times per condition for statistical significance.
claims.poster_quote: Experiments were repeated 10 times per condition for statistical significance.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: To create statistical significance every experiment is repeated ten times.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that experiments were repeated 10 times per condition for statistical significance.

claims.text: The setup enabled precise quantification of slippage, trajectory deviation, and critical failure thresholds.
claims.poster_quote: The setup enabled precise quantification of slippage, trajectory deviation, and critical failure thresholds.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The setup enabled precise quantification of slippage, trajectory deviation, and critical failure thresholds.
claims.reason: The paper confirms that the setup enabled precise quantification of these metrics.

claims.text: Friction alone cannot predict locomotion success—dynamic load redistribution and control matter more.
claims.poster_quote: (1) Friction alone cannot predict locomotion success—dynamic load redistribution and control matter more.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Dynamic locomotion performance cannot be predicted from friction measurements alone. The measured dynamic coefficients of friction suggest theoretically achievable incline angles above 48◦ , yet locomotion failed at substantially lower slopes.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that friction alone cannot predict locomotion success and highlights the importance of dynamic factors.

claims.text: Center-of-mass shifts toward rear legs on inclines reduce front-foot friction, requiring incline-aware control.
claims.poster_quote: (2) Center-of-mass shifts toward rear legs on inclines reduce front-foot friction, requiring incline-aware control.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: As incline angle increases, the center of mass shifts toward the rear legs, reducing normal forces and therefore friction forces at the front feet.
claims.reason: The paper discusses center-of-mass shifts reducing front-foot friction on inclines.

claims.text: Discrete terrain features (tile steps, curves) dominate slip events, demanding perception and precise foothold selection.
claims.poster_quote: (3) Discrete terrain features (tile steps, curves) dominate slip events, demanding perception and precise foothold selection.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Slippage was frequently triggered by abrupt slip-off events at tile steps and curved sections, even on 0◦ incline.
claims.reason: The paper confirms that discrete terrain features dominate slip events.

claims.text: Standard controllers apply uniform push-off forces, exceeding friction cones on slopes—adaptive gait parameters are essential.
claims.poster_quote: (4) Standard controllers apply uniform push-off forces, exceeding friction cones on slopes—adaptive gait parameters are essential.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The evaluated controller applied similar push-off forces and gait timing across all inclines. This resulted in tangential forces exceeding the friction cone on steeper slopes.
claims.reason: The paper states that standard controllers apply uniform push-off forces, exceeding friction cones on slopes.

claims.text: Ball feet’s small contact area and lack of terrain adaptation are critical hardware limitations.
claims.poster_quote: (5) Ball feet’s small contact area and lack of terrain adaptation are critical hardware limitations; future designs need larger, high-friction, interlocking surfaces.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Ball-shaped feet exhibited systematic limitations due to their small contact area and lack of geometric adaptation to tiled surfaces.
claims.reason: The paper identifies ball feet’s small contact area and lack of terrain adaptation as critical hardware limitations.

claims.text: Future designs need larger, high-friction, interlocking surfaces.
claims.poster_quote: (5) Ball feet’s small contact area and lack of terrain adaptation are critical hardware limitations; future designs need larger, high-friction, interlocking surfaces.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Future robot feet for roof environments should be equipped with a larger, adaptable contact area, high friction materials, and actuated ankle joints to allow for more stable positioning of the body.
claims.reason: The paper suggests future designs need larger, high-friction, interlocking surfaces.

claims.text: Get-up/lie-down motions must be terrain-aware or restricted to level surfaces.
claims.poster_quote: (6) Get-up/lie-down motions must be terrain-aware or restricted to level surfaces.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Get-up and lie-down motions failed at very low inclines because the pre-programmed sequences do not consider body orientation relative to gravity.
claims.reason: The paper states that get-up/lie-down motions must be terrain-aware or restricted to level surfaces.

claims.text: The Go2 failed to meet manufacturer claims of 40° slope capability.
claims.poster_quote: The Go2 failed to meet manufacturer claims of 40° slope capability.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Manufacturer claims of slope-climbing capabilities of up to 40◦ were not achieved under the test conditions [18].
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that the Go2 failed to meet manufacturer claims of 40° slope capability.

claims.text: Standing balance failed at 27.58° ± 0.72°, primarily due to front-limb slippage.
claims.poster_quote: Standing balance failed at 27.58° ± 0.72°, primarily due to front-limb slippage.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: For standing on an incline, the critical angle was measured at (27.58 ± 0.72)◦ on average.
claims.reason: The paper provides the exact measurement for standing balance failure at 27.58° ± 0.72°.

claims.text: Get-up/lie-down succeeded only up to 11° (head-up/down) and 7° (sideways).
claims.poster_quote: Get-up/lie-down succeeded only up to 11° (head-up/down) and 7° (sideways), failing when the center of mass exited the support polygon.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Full task success was achieved only at low inclines: up to 11.0◦ for head-up and head-down orientations, and up to 7.0◦ for the sideways orientation.
claims.reason: The paper provides the exact incline angles for successful get-up/lie-down sequences.

claims.text: Incline walking showed a quadratic increase in slippage with incline angle (p < 0.001).
claims.poster_quote: Incline walking showed a quadratic increase in slippage with incline angle (p < 0.001), with critical failures occurring regularly at 25°.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Regression analysis revealed [...] a highly significant (p(F ) < 0.001) quadratic relationship between incline angle and slippage.
claims.reason: The paper confirms a quadratic increase in slippage with incline angle (p < 0.001).

claims.text: Critical failures occurred regularly at 25° incline during walking.
claims.poster_quote: Incline walking showed a quadratic increase in slippage with incline angle (p < 0.001), with critical failures occurring regularly at 25°.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Incline walking was evaluated by repeatedly ascending increasingly higher slopes while measuring slippage [...] with frequent falls observed at 25◦.
claims.reason: The paper states that critical failures occurred regularly at 25° incline during walking.

claims.text: Even on flat ground, tile steps caused slippage.
claims.poster_quote: Even on flat ground, tile steps caused slippage.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The roof environment makes the robot slip even on flat ground, due to the small steps between individual rows of tiles.
claims.reason: The paper confirms that tile steps caused slippage even on flat ground.

claims.text: Regression analysis confirmed a linear decrease in traveled distance.
claims.poster_quote: Regression analysis confirmed a linear decrease in traveled distance and no significant correlation with trajectory deviation.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Regression analysis revealed a highly significant (p < 0.0035) linear relationship between incline angle and traveled distance.
claims.reason: The paper confirms a linear decrease in traveled distance via regression analysis.

claims.text: Regression analysis found no significant correlation with trajectory deviation.
claims.poster_quote: Regression analysis confirmed a linear decrease in traveled distance and no significant correlation with trajectory deviation.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Regression analysis found no explainable correlation between incline angle and trajectory deviation.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that no significant correlation was found with trajectory deviation.

claims.text: Friction coefficients were 1.144 (flat) and 1.430 (curved).

claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The coefficient of friction for a rubber ball foot on a roof tile was measured at 1.144 ± 0.1299 on flat and 1.430 ± 0.1298 on curved sections of the roof.
claims.reason: The paper provides the exact friction coefficients for flat and curved surfaces.

claims.text: Theoretical inclines >48° were suggested by friction coefficients, but dynamic performance fell far short.
claims.poster_quote: Friction coefficients were 1.144 (flat) and 1.430 (curved), suggesting theoretical inclines >48°, but dynamic performance fell far short—highlighting control and stability as key bottlenecks.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The measured dynamic coefficients of friction suggest theoretically achievable incline angles above 48◦ , yet locomotion failed at substantially lower slopes.
claims.reason: The paper states theoretical inclines >48° were suggested by friction coefficients, but dynamic performance fell far short.

claims.text: Dynamic performance was limited by control and stability bottlenecks.
claims.poster_quote: Friction coefficients were 1.144 (flat) and 1.430 (curved), suggesting theoretical inclines >48°, but dynamic performance fell far short—highlighting control and stability as key bottlenecks.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The experiments highlight that roof locomotion is strongly limited by dynamic stability and control, but also by material friction.
claims.reason: The paper identifies control and stability bottlenecks as limiting dynamic performance.

claims.text: Future work should integrate reinforcement learning for slope-adaptive gaits.
